PHSCS 587

Fermi–Dirac occupation

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how the Fermi level and thermal broadening determine state occupation

To predict charge population, first ask whether a state exists and then whether it is occupied. At thermal equilibrium the expected electron occupation of an available state of energy E is f(E) = 1/{1 + exp[(E − EF)/(kBT)]}. EF is the chemical potential, kB is Boltzmann’s constant, and T is absolute temperature in kelvin. E, EF and kBT must use the same energy unit.

The energy zero is a choice of ruler. Adding the same constant to E and EF leaves E − EF unchanged, so the occupation probability stays the same. When comparing two positions in a connected device, use one common energy reference. At each position, the local separation EC − EF sets the equilibrium conduction-band population; the material bandgap EC − EV describes a different separation.

At finite temperature f(EF) = 1/2, and the transition spans an energy scale of a few kBT. A Fermi level within a bandgap remains a useful chemical potential even though no bulk band state exists at that exact energy. In the zero-temperature limit the distribution becomes a step: allowed states below EF are occupied and those above it are empty.

High above EF, where E − EF is several kBT, f(E) approaches exp[−(E − EF)/(kBT)], the Boltzmann tail. This approximation enables familiar exponential carrier formulas. Carrier density still requires a density-of-states integral; a probability by itself has no units of carriers per volume.

Example

At E = EF + 2kBT, the exact occupation is 1/(1 + e²) ≈ 0.119. The Boltzmann value e⁻² ≈ 0.135 already shows a visible approximation error.

Practice

1. Does f(EF) = 1/2 imply a half-occupied band state when EF lies in a gap?

Separate available states from their occupation.

The formula assigns a probability conditional on a state existing. An ideal gap has zero band DOS, so it contributes no band carriers at EF.
